sections.summary: TSMC disclosed that its consolidated net revenue for August 2026 reached NT$514.81 billion, a 53.3 % increase from August 2025 and a 10.1 % rise from July 2026, while the January‑August run‑rate hit NT$3,386.87 billion, up 39.3 % year‑on‑year. In the second quarter, net profit surged 77 % to NT$706.56 billion, driving earnings per share to NT$27.25, and employee bonuses for the first half of the year climbed 54.3 % to NT$70.35 billion. The company also announced an additional US$100 billion investment in its Arizona operations, bringing its total U.S. commitment to US$265 billion to fund new fabs, advanced packaging and expanded capacity. Furthermore, TSMC detailed intra‑group financing and guarantees supporting subsidiaries in North America, Global Operations and Arizona, underscoring its ongoing capital deployment to reinforce overseas manufacturing and the global chip supply chain.

sections.title: Operational disruptions
sections.note: Track logistics, outages, and supply constraints.
sections.summary: Recent developments underscore that Taiwan’s dominance in advanced chip manufacturing makes any interruption to TSMC’s operations a systemic risk for global technology supply chains. Elon Musk warned that a disruption in the Taiwan Strait could cripple the AI‑chip market, noting that TSMC supplies the bulk of the most advanced nodes used by Nvidia and other AI designers; the warning prompted massive investment in a Texas “Terafab” as a partial “self‑rescue” strategy, although experts caution that replicating TSMC’s decades‑long process expertise will take years. In parallel, TSMC’s key supplier Nichias has begun constructing a new plant in Hsinchu to produce PFA tubes—critical plastic components for moving chemicals inside fabs—to pre‑empt bottlenecks that have previously slowed capacity expansions. China has also begun selectively slowing shipments of germanium, quartz and permanent‑magnet materials to Taiwan, creating additional supply constraints for semiconductor fabrication and related optical‑photonics production. These geopolitical and material‑supply pressures have reinforced the concept of Taiwan’s “silicon shield,” where the world’s reliance on TSMC’s sub‑7 nm chips raises the economic cost of any conflict, yet the shield alone cannot guarantee stability. Consequently, governments and companies are accelerating diversification: TSMC is expanding U.S. capacity in Arizona and Texas, while regional alliances such as the SEMI chip‑materials coalition aim to localise raw‑material supplies and reduce dependence on vulnerable imports. Overall, while TSMC’s domestic production remains the linchpin of global AI and advanced‑chip supply, a combination of geopolitical tension, export‑control frictions and material shortages continues to threaten uninterrupted output, prompting a multi‑pronged push for capacity outside Taiwan and stronger supply‑chain resilience.

sections.summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) is subject to U.S. export‑control measures that limit its ability to supply advanced‑node semiconductor manufacturing equipment and related software to China, including new Foreign Direct Product (FDP) rules that extend jurisdiction over foreign‑produced tools when they are destined for the People’s Republic of China; the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security also closed the Validated End‑User (VEU) loophole in August 2025, requiring foreign‑owned fabs in China to obtain licenses for such exports, and TSMC appears on the Bureau’s EAR Part 740 list of approved ultimate consignees for advanced‑computing items, indicating that while it can receive certain U.S.‑origin items under license exceptions, any shipments of equipment capable of producing advanced chips for military or AI applications must be authorized and are tightly restricted.
